Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) currently faces a dual challenge regarding dataset utilization. First, the reliance on massive pre-collected datasets incurs substantial computational costs during training. Second, and perhaps more critically, the inclusion of all available data is often counterproductive; "more" is not necessarily "better." Suboptimal or noisy trajectories within a large dataset can exacerbate distribution shift issues, leading the agent to learn degraded policies compared to what could be achieved with a cleaner, smaller set. There is currently no established framework in offline RL for systematically identifying the "minimal effective subset" that maximizes performance while minimizing training overhead.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the information necessary to train a robust offline RL agent is contained within a small fraction of the total dataset. Specifically, we propose that if a reduced data subset yields loss gradients that closely approximate the gradients of the full dataset, a policy trained on this subset will achieve comparable—or potentially superior—performance. We posit that the standard Actor-Critic learning objective can be reformulated as a submodular optimization problem, allowing us to use greedy algorithms to identify the most "informative" trajectories while filtering out data that contributes to negative distribution shift.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a method named **ReDOR (Reduced Datasets for Offline RL)**. Our approach treats dataset selection not as a random sampling task, but as a gradient matching optimization problem.

1.  **Gradient Approximation Formulation:**
    We will define an objective function where the goal is to select a subset of data (and associated weights) such that the weighted sum of their gradients minimizes the Euclidean distance to the gradient of the entire dataset. This ensures the training signal remains consistent with the global objective.

2.  **Iterative Greedy Selection (Orthogonal Matching Pursuit):**
    Since finding the optimal subset is computationally intractable (NP-Hard), we will employ a greedy iterative strategy. We will adapt Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) to select data points one by one. At each step, the algorithm will select the data point whose gradient vector best correlates with the current residual error of the gradient approximation.

3.  **Stabilization for Reinforcement Learning:**
    Unlike supervised learning, RL targets (Q-values) are non-stationary and shift as the policy updates. To prevent this instability from ruining the data selection process, we propose three specific modifications:
    *   **Empirical Return Smoothing:** Instead of relying solely on the fluctuating TD-error gradients, we will incorporate empirical trajectory returns to provide a stable target proxy during the selection phase.
    *   **Multi-Round Selection:** We will perform the subset selection periodically over multiple rounds. This allows the dataset to evolve dynamically, capturing different critical samples as the agent's understanding of the value function matures.
    *   **Trajectory-Based Granularity:** To preserve temporal coherence, we will enforce selection at the *trajectory* level rather than individual transitions. The mean gradient of a trajectory will serve as the basis vector for the matching pursuit.

4.  **Quality Bias Constraint:**
    To explicitly combat distribution shift, we will bias the matching process. We will introduce a constraint that prioritizes selecting trajectories with higher estimated returns, ensuring the gradient matching doesn't accidentally force the agent to mimic low-quality behavior just to satisfy the mathematical approximation.

## Expected Contribution
We expect this work to pioneer the study of dataset reduction specifically for offline RL. Theoretically, we aim to bridge the gap between submodular optimization (typically used in supervised learning) and the dynamic objectives of RL. Practically, this approach intends to demonstrate that training on a carefully pruned subset can significantly reduce computational runtime while simultaneously improving policy performance by removing detrimental data points. This could fundamentally change how large-scale offline RL datasets are curated and utilized.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method (REDOR) against various baselines in offline reinforcement learning environments. The experiments were designed to assess performance improvements, data selection efficacy, and computational complexity.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **D4RL Benchmark:** We utilized the standard D4RL datasets (Fu et al., 2020).
    *   **D4RL (Hard):** We constructed a more challenging scenario by adding additional low-quality data to the standard datasets to simulate noise in real-world tasks.
    *   **Antmaze:** We included Antmaze tasks (umaze, medium-play, large-play, and diverse variants) to test generalization and trajectory stitching capabilities.
    *   **Specific Domains:** Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah, Antmaze.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Normalized Score:** We calculated the return of 10 episodes per evaluation point. Results report the average and standard deviation over five independent random seeds.
    *   **Computational Complexity:** Measured in minutes required for data selection on specific dataset sizes.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **RL-Specific Data Selection:**
        *   *Complete Dataset:* Training on the full, original dataset.
        *   *Prioritized:* Based on Prioritized Experience Replay, selecting samples with the highest TD losses.
        *   *Random:* Randomly selecting subsets of the same size as the proposed method.
    *   **Supervised Learning (SL) Reduction Techniques:**
        *   *KRLS:* Kernel Recursive Least Squares (coherence criterion).
        *   *Log-Det:* Informative Vector Machines (geometric criterion).
        *   *BlockGreedy:* Adapting kernel representation.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** All experiments were conducted on a GeForce RTX 3090 GPU.
    *   **Backbone Algorithms:**
        *   For Mujoco/D4RL tasks: TD3+BC (Fujimoto & Gu, 2021).
        *   For Antmaze tasks: IQL (Implicit Q-Learning).
    *   **Training Parameters:**
        *   Training steps: 1 million.
        *   Evaluation frequency: Every 5,000 steps.
        *   Optimizer: Adam.
        *   Learning Rates: 3e-4 (Actor and Critic).
        *   Batch Size: 256.
        *   Discount Factor: 0.99.
        *   Target Update Rate: 5e-3.
        *   Policy Noise: 0.2; Clipping: (-0.5, 0.5).
        *   TD3+BC Regularization Parameter: 2.5.
        *   Network Architecture: 2 hidden layers of 256 dim, ReLU activation.
    *   **REDOR Specific Parameters:**
        *   Training rounds ($T$): 50.
        *   Per-round selection ($m$): 50.
        *   Epsilon ($\epsilon$): 0.01.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

We derived the following observations from the textual analysis of results, learning curves, and ablation studies:

*   **General Performance vs. Baselines (D4RL Hard):**
    *   We observed that the proposed method consistently achieved superior performance compared to the Complete Dataset, Prioritized, and Random baselines in the Mujoco domain.
    *   Agents learning from the reduced dataset generated by our method demonstrated faster learning convergence than those learning from the complete dataset.
    *   The Supervised Learning baselines (KRLS, Log-Det, BlockGreedy) generally underperformed compared to our method. This suggests that static data selection methods are ill-suited for Offline RL where target values evolve dynamically.

*   **Performance in Sparse Reward Settings (Antmaze):**
    *   In Antmaze tasks, which require trajectory stitching, random data removal resulted in the loss of critical data, preventing task completion.
    *   Our method outperformed the Complete Dataset in Antmaze environments, indicating it successfully balanced data quantity with performance and retained valuable trajectories for stitching.

*   **Ablation Study Findings:**
    *   **Single Round Selection:** Removing the multi-round selection strategy significantly degraded performance. In the `walker2d-medium` task, performance decreased by over 80% without multi-round selection.
    *   **Q-Target Stabilization:** Replacing empirical returns with standard Q-targets caused instability. In the `walker2d-expert` task, this ablation resulted in a 95% performance drop.
    *   **Task Sensitivity:** In `halfcheetah` tasks, the impact of removing these modules was smaller, likely due to the limited state space allowing easier identification of diverse data.

*   **Visual Analysis of Selected Data (t-SNE):**
    *   The dataset embedding revealed segmentation into diverse components corresponding to distinct agent skills (e.g., falling, leg lifting, jumping, landing).
    *   Samples selected by our method effectively bridged the gaps between these components, enhancing versatility.
    *   Specifically, our method selected fewer data points associated with "falling" and focused more on task-relevant data, explaining the performance improvement over the full dataset.

*   **Computational Efficiency:**
    *   Despite processing datasets with millions of data points, the computational overhead remained low (between 3 to 14 minutes depending on dataset size).
    *   This efficiency is attributed to the trajectory-based selection technique and the regularized constraint technique.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}

\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\

Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format

1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---

Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.

The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shifted the paradigm from real-time interaction to learning from pre-collected datasets. However, this approach faces two critical limitations. First, reliance on massive datasets incurs substantial computational costs during policy learning, particularly when extensive hyperparameter tuning is required. Second, and perhaps more critically, simply adding more data does not guarantee improved performance; the inclusion of suboptimal trajectories can exacerbate distribution shift issues, leading to policy degradation.

A fundamental gap exists in determining the "minimal sufficient" data requirements for offline RL. While data subset selection is well-explored in supervised learning, it cannot be directly applied to RL. In supervised learning, targets are static, whereas in RL, target values (and thus gradients) evolve as the policy updates. We lack a rigorous framework to select a subset of the offline dataset that enhances algorithm performance while significantly reducing training time, specifically one that accounts for the non-stationary nature of RL targets.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can identify an optimal subset $\mathcal{S}$ of a complete offline dataset $\mathcal{D}$ by framing dataset selection as a **gradient approximation optimization problem**.

Our core premise is that if the weighted gradients of the Temporal Difference (TD) loss on a reduced dataset $\mathcal{S}$ can closely approximate the gradients calculated on the full dataset $\mathcal{D}$, training on $\mathcal{S}$ will yield a Q-function and policy nearly identical (or superior, due to noise reduction) to those trained on $\mathcal{D}$. To make this tractable, we posit that the Actor-Critic framework can be reformulated as a **submodular optimization objective**, allowing us to solve the selection problem using a modified Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP). Furthermore, we hypothesize that to handle the moving target problem in RL, we must match gradients based on **empirical returns** rather than bootstrapping, and select data at the **trajectory level** rather than the transition level.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a method named **ReDOR** (Reduced Datasets for Offline RL). The methodology consists of three phases: mathematical formulation of the gradient matching problem, proving the submodularity of the RL objective to justify a greedy approach, and specific architectural modifications to OMP to handle RL dynamics.

### 1. Gradient Approximation Formulation
Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^M$ denote the complete dataset. We aim to find a subset $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$ and associated weights $\mathbf{w}$ to minimize the difference between the gradients derived from the subset and the full dataset.

We define the standard Q-learning TD loss over the full dataset as:
$$ \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}} \mathcal{L}^i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathtt{TD}}(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i, \boldsymbol{\theta}) $$
where $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ represents the network parameters.

We define the loss on the reduced subset $\mathcal{S}$ with weights $w_i$ as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rdc}}(\pmb{w}, \theta) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} w_i \mathcal{L}^i(\theta) $$

Our objective is to minimize the gradient approximation error, defined as:
$$ \mathrm{Err}\left({\pmb w}, {\pmb S}, {\pmb \mathcal{L}}, \theta \right) = \| \sum_{i \in {\pmb S}} w_i \nabla_{\theta} {\pmb \mathcal{L}}^i \left(\theta\right) - \nabla_{\theta} {\pmb \mathcal{L}} \left(\theta\right) \|_2 $$

To enforce sparsity and prevent overfitting, we will minimize a regularized error term:
$$ \mathrm{Err}_{\lambda}\left(\pmb{w}, \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{L}, \theta\right) = \mathrm{Err}\left(\pmb{w}, \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{L}, \theta\right) + \lambda \|\pmb{w}\|_2^2 $$
where $\lambda$ is a regularization coefficient.

### 2. Submodular Optimization & Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP)
Directly optimizing the selection of $\mathcal{S}$ is NP-hard. We will solve this by proving that the objective function $F_{\lambda}(S) = L_{\mathrm{max}} - \min_w \mathrm{Err}_{\lambda}(w, S, \mathcal{L}, \theta)$ is weakly submodular. This justification allows us to use **Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP)**, a greedy iterative algorithm, to select data points.

We will formally define the submodularity for both the Critic ($Q$) and Actor ($\pi$) components. For a subset size bounded by $N$, assuming bounded TD loss ($U_{\mathrm{TD}}$) and gradients ($U_{\nabla Q}$), we will establish that the Critic objective $F_{\lambda}^Q(S)$ is $\delta$-weakly submodular with:
$$ \delta \ge \frac{\lambda}{\lambda + 4N(U_{\tt TD} U_{\nabla Q})^2} $$
Similarly, for the Actor, we will derive a corresponding bound based on action divergence constraints.

### 3. Modifications for Offline RL Stability
Standard OMP fails in RL because $\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}$ fluctuates as the target Q-values change. We will implement three critical modifications to the standard OMP algorithm:

**A. Stabilization via Empirical Returns**
Instead of matching gradients of the unstable TD loss, we will match gradients derived from empirical returns. This provides a consistent learning signal. We define the target $y$ as the discounted sum of rewards within the trajectory:
$$ \nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}\left(\theta\right) = \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[(y - Q_{\theta}(s_t, a_t))^2], \quad y = \sum_{k=0}^{H-t} \gamma^k r(s_{t+k}, a_{t+k}) $$

**B. Multi-Round Selection Strategy**
To capture the evolution of the policy, we will not select data based on a single snapshot of $\theta$. Instead, we will perform selection over $T$ rounds. We will pre-store parameters $\theta_t$ from a preliminary run and select a portion of the subset at each round $t$ based on $\nabla_{\theta_t} \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)$.

**C. Trajectory-Based Selection**
Offline RL data is sequential. Selecting isolated transitions breaks temporal coherence. We will modify OMP to select entire trajectories. For a new trajectory $i$ of length $K$, we will use the mean gradient as the basis vector:
$$ \nabla_{\theta_t} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Traj}}^i\left(\theta_t\right) = \sum_{k=1}^K \nabla_{\theta_t} \mathcal{L}^k\left(\theta_t\right) / K $$
The OMP algorithm will iteratively select the trajectory that maximizes the inner product with the current residual error.

### 4. Quality-Constraint Integration
Finally, to mitigate distribution shift caused by suboptimal data, we will impose a constraint that biases the gradient matching towards high-performing trajectories. We will restrict the calculation of the target gradient $\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta)$ to include only trajectories where the return satisfies:
$$ y > \mathrm{Top}\ m\%(\{ \mathrm{Return}(\mathrm{Trajectory}_j) \}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}) $$
This ensures the reduced dataset $\mathcal{S}$ focuses on reconstructing the gradients of the best-performing data, implicitly filtering out noise.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Framework:** We will provide the first theoretical analysis demonstrating that the dataset selection problem in Actor-Critic frameworks can be transformed into a submodular optimization problem, complete with derivation of approximation bounds and convergence properties.
2.  **Algorithmic Innovation:** We will propose ReDOR, a novel algorithm that adapts Orthogonal Matching Pursuit to the non-stationary domain of Reinforcement Learning by introducing empirical return smoothing and trajectory-based selection.
3.  **Efficiency & Scalability:** We expect this method to drastically reduce the size of offline datasets required for training (lowering computational cost) while maintaining or exceeding the performance of policies trained on the full dataset by effectively filtering suboptimal trajectories.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.

notes.model: claude-sonnet-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
